speechtext: BORDElN. I would like to ask the government whether all the measures in the shape of legislation which are to be brought down this session are before the House, and if not, what other measures, if any, the government propose to bring down?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think there are perhaps one or two minor measures to be brought down, and we propose an amendment to the election law, which will be brought down at a very early day, and perhaps another measure, the tenor of which I will give my hou. friend later on.

House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Fielding :
That the Speaker do now leave the chair, for the House to go into committee to consider of the ways and means for raising the supply to he granted to His Majesty.
['INGRAM (East Elgin) moved the adjournment of the debate.\nMotion agreed to and debate adjourned.\nOn motion of Mr. Fielding, House adjourned at 11.30 p.m.', 'Wednesday, June 15, 1904.']

In resuming. Mr. Speaker, the debate on the fiscal policy of the government, I wish to state at the outset that in my opinion the budget is one of which the hon. the Finance Minister has every reason to be proud. It is one which, I believe, the country will cordially and heartily endorse, and on which the Liberal party lias reason to congratulate itself and the country. It is a budget that will bring to every patriotic Canadian a sense of pleasure and gratification, a

feeling of confidence and hopefulness for the future and the assurance that the affairs of this Dominion are in good hands and will continue to be managed in the best interests of the people. I. well remember a prophecy made on the accession of the Liberal party to power by one who proved himself a false prophet, that the Liberal party would not be able to govern the country more than six months. Our record, Sir, of the eight past years flatly contradicts that prediction, and shows that the affairs-of this country have been well managed and are perfectly safe in the hands of the Liberal party.
The hon. member for South Simcoe ('Mr. Lennox), in the course of his remarks, said be would not discuss the budget at length, because there was nothing in it. Well, Mr. Speaker, I would ask is it nothing that the Finance Minister was able last year to announce a surplus of over $14,000,000 ? Is it nothing that he is able to estimate this year a surplus of $10,500,000, the largest in the history of the Dominion ? Is it nothing that the Finance Minister has been able to announce substantial surpluses seven years in succession, and that the total of these amounts to over $57,000,000? Is it a fact not worth mentioning that we have been able to deepen our canals, enlarge and improve our harbours, extend the Intercolonial, erect the necessary public buildings in various parts of the Dominion, and carry on the general affairs of the country without adding one cent 'to our taxation ? Is it nothing that the Finance Minister has been able to announce a reduction of over $1,000,000 in the public debt this year below what it was when the Liberal party took office ? Is it nothing to be able to prove that while the Conservatives added an average of $6,500,000 to the debt every year for the eighteen years they were in office, the Liberals have not added one single cent ? Is it nothing that the per capita debt to-day is only $46 f.s compared with $50 in 1896 ? Is it a fact not worth noting that our commercial prosperity to-day is not only greater than it ever has been in our history, but exceeds that of any other country in the world ? Is it a matter of no consequence that our imports are $241,000,000 to-day as against less than $120,000,000 eight years ago, and that our exports are nearly $230,000,000 as against $121,000,000 eight years ago ? Is it nothing that our total trade, which is the barometer of a country's prosperity, amounts to $467,000,000 to-day as compared with $224,000,000 in 1896, being an increase of $243,000,000, and that our increase alone is $19,000,000 ever the total trade of 1896 ? Is it nothing that our export trade with the mother country is $63,000,000 more than it was eight years ago, and that our total trade with the mother country is $88,000,000 more than it was in 1896, and that, in fact, our increase is as large as our entire trade with that country was in 1895 ? Are we to be told that it is really of no account whatever that Mr. HOLMES.
cur railway tonnage should be 23,000,000 more than it was eight years ago and that our business failures are $8,000,000 less in value than they were eight years ago, and much less than at any time during the last twenty-one years ? Is it nothing that the deposits in our chartered banks to-day are $196,000,000 more than they were in 1896. the increase alone being greater than the total deposits in that year ? Is it nothing that the deposits in our savings banks amount to $21,000,000 more than they did in 1896 V Yet in the face of all these incontrovertible evidences of marvellous and unequalled prosperity of this wisely and well governed Dominion, there are some members who have the audacity to say of the best budget ever brought down, ' there is nothing in it.'
My hon. friend from South Wentworth (Mr. E. D. Smith), who preceded me in this debate, endeavoured to belittle the administration of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) in so far as the hon. minister had endeavoured to do something for the farmers. The hon. gentleman, in an interesting speech from the standpoint of a fruit exporter, dealt with the question of cold storage and its effect on the transport of apples and other perishable fruits. With that question I do not purpose dealing, because I think there are others in this House who are more competent to discuss it, but I would make a brief reference to the course which the1 hon. Minister of Agriculture took with regard to the quarantine. The hon. member for South Wentworth endeavoured to belittle what the hon. minister did, and in order to give point to his arguments he sought to convey the idea that because our exports of cattle to the United States last year were smaller than in other years, therefore the Minister of Agriculture had accomplished nothing in the interests of the farmers. But he omitted to tell this House that in the four and a half years which preceded the removal of the quarantine-the removal of which was brought about, as everybody knows, through the efforts of the Minister of Agriculture-we only sent to the United States 3,672 head of cattle, or an average of a little over 700 head, and that in the succeeding four years, after the removal of the quarantine, we sent an average of 87,343, or a total value of $5,329,000. Nor did he inform the House that prior to the removal of the quarantine our farmers had on hand a large number of Stockers, which were of comparatively small value, and for which they had no market at the time ; and while I would agree with him that it would be wise for our farmers to feed all their cattle possible on their own farms, it is my firm conviction that the price of the stockers has increased by virtue of the removal of the quarantine, as our farmers now enjoy the benefit of an increased market, and there is no demand in the United States for stockers which there was a short time ago.

He also dealt with the question of an increase in the duty on market-garden products. He was very earnest in his advocacy of the claims of the market-gardener, hut as that question has been dealt with recently from this side of the House, I do not propose to weary the House by entering into it again. I would only call attention to the fact that my hon. friend, who is an exporter of fruit, makes as much use of the American market as is possible under present circumstances, and I do not think he would like to toe thrown out of that market, to which market-gardeners from the Niagara section have convenient access. And he also endeavoured to convince us that it would be the part of wisdom for the government to increase the tariff so far as small fruits are concerned. He laid special stress upon the fact that California fruit was preferred in the west and more especially in Winnipeg, over Canadian fruits. But he did not tell this House, as he might have done, that one reason for this is that the Canadian packers do not take quite the same interest, I am sorry to say, in placing their fruit properly on the market that the California Fruit Agency does. It is a well known fact, and I am not impugning the Canadian packer. But those who have made inquiries for fruit sent out by the California fruit agency know that that fruit can be depended upon to be exactly what it is represented. And, by this means, the California people have established themselves in the western market while our Canadian packers have not met the conditions by proper care with reference to packages and the putting up of the fruit. Now, let me call attention to the duties that are now charged upon some of these articles. The duty on peaches coming into Canada is ouet cent a pound. The duty on plums is 25 per cent. The hon. gentleman (Mr. E. D. Smith) instanced plums in particular. The Canadian plum is admitted to be superior in flavour to the American1 plum, but they cannot be transported with the same degree of ease, and that is one reason why they do not get the preference in the market. The duty on tomatoes is 20 cents per bushel, and 10 per cent ad valorem. The duty on grapes is 2 cents per pound. Now, I am not a consumer of grapes to any great extent, but I think I know something of the conditions of the market. I believe I am not underestimating the value when I say that, in certain seasons of the year and in certain sections of the province of Ontario, grapes are sold as low as 2 cents per pound. At- those seasons, the duty represents 100 per cent. It seems to me that, on some lines of fruit, the duty is large enough. On blackberries, gooseberries, raspberries, strawberries, cherries and currants, the duty is 2 cents per pound. Cranberries, plums and quinces, 25 per cent. Prunes, including raisins, dried currants and California or silver prunes, 1 cent per pound. The hon. gentleman (Mr. E. D. Smith) laid great stress upon the opinion that we ought to look after the producers, and said that if we looked after the producer the consumer would be able to look after himself. Well, I think there are times when it is right to look after the producer, but there are certainly times when it is the duty of the government to look after the consumer as well. The consumer has interests that deserve consideration as well as those of the producer. I do not know but that sometimes the hon. gentleman's expression could be reversed and that, with regard to some things in Canada, if we look after the consumer the producer is able to look after himself. The producer is less important, certainly so far as numbers are concerned. It is the duty of the government to look after the consumer as well as the producer.
Then, the hon. gentleman from South Wentworth dwelt at length on the argument that we ought to protect the farmers.
I think the time has come, so far as the general principle is concerned, when we ought to cease statements of that kind in this House. I think almost everybody will admit that, so far as protection to the farmers is concerned, we can do comparatively little. We may do something but, generally speaking we cannot protect the farmer. And I think the House knows that perfectly well, and that the members of tha opposition know it as well as we do, and,
I think, in private conversation they would be prepared to admit it. But, in connection with their argument in favour of protection to all classes they feel it necessary to advocate protection to the farmer though they know that it cannot be carried out to its logical conclusion.
Now, one of the important features of the budget is the reduction of the duty on coal oil. I do not profess to be an oil man or to know much of the oil trade, beyond what I have read in the newspapers and gathered from conversation. I am free to admit that the newspapers are not always reliable. Sometimes, their statements are hardly in accordance with the facts. For instance, I read in the Hamilton ' Spectator ' the following*;
The reduction in the duty on coal oil amounts to exactly nothing. The Standard Oil Company may want It for its own purposes ; but the people of Canada will benefit not a cent from it.
Then, in the Ottawa ' Free Press,' the day after the change was made in the coal oil duties I find this advertisement;

We have reduced our prices on all grades of refined oil, benzine and gasoline 2J cents per gallon in consequence of a reduction of the same amount made in the tariff.
The Queen City Oil Company, Limited.

I also read in interviews the opinions of producers who are, apparently, in sympathy with a reduction of the duties. The Toronto ' News,' no matter what may be the personal opinion of the editor, is not a paper that is regarded as especially friendly to the Liberal party. It is well known that the proprietor is a Conservative, and therefore, we must count the paper as an ^independent paper with Conservative leanings. Speaking of the oil duties, it says :
The immediate changes are regarded as undoubtedly a step in the right direction. The reduction of duty on refined oil is excusable by the fact that Canadian oil wells and refineries are not able to produce sufficient oil to^ supply the market, while the placing of fuel oil for manufacturing purposes on the free list will be of the greatest assistance to manufacturing interests.
The needs of the oil refiners are met by cutting the duty in two, while the domestic producer is rewarded with a bounty. The price of oil to the consumer should fall at once.

Gall, of the Gall, Schneider Company, makes this statement:
Every consumer of coal oil in Canada will now be able to get oil at least 2J cents cheaper per gallon, and a further reduction may be possible as soon as the question of the bounty adjusts itself.
Mr. Fairbank, who is spoken of as one of the largest oil producers in the Petrolia section, is quoted thus :
J. H. Fairbank said he thought it a wise piece of legislatiou on the part of the' government, and that from the information at hand the crude producers would not materially suffer.
The argument has been advanced that the effect of the reduction in the duty on oil will be to endanger the oil business in Lambton and other counties in western Ontario. I do not suppose that any one will call in question the party fealty of the Petrolea correspondent of the Toronto ' Mail and Empire.' I assume that this correspondent Is a Conservative and voices the sentiments of his political friends. Speaking of the reduction of the duty on coal oil this correspondent, as will be seen in the ' Mail and Empire ' of June 9th makes the following statement :
The fact that the government had announced a bounty of 1J cents per gallon on all crude oil produced from this date did not at first strike the minds of the inhabitants, and it was felt that the town had received a blow which it would take years to recover from. This morning, however, it was realized that while the situation is not to the liking of the inhabitants, it is not as bad as It might be. The price of crude oil yesterday morning was reduced from $2.09 per barrel to $2.06, and this 'morning a further drop was announced to $1.65 per barrel, but this later figure is supplemented by the bounty of 521 cents to be paid by the government, making the price now $2.17J per barrel.
If the producer had any guarantee of the length of time the government would keep the bounty Mr. HOLMES.
in force, he would feel much easier in his mind	 Leading producers are all rather chary at the present time of expressing an opinion, but whatever the outcome, the people of the town will not be knocked out by the blow, but will go ahead and develop oil territory wherever they can get it, and will try and make the production reach the present and future wants of the people.
So, on that point at any rate, this correspondent who I presume is a Conservative, [DOT]speaks rather favourably, if we read between the lines.
I have here one or two other expressions of opinion from producers about Petrolia similar to those of Mr. Fairbank. It is not necessary to quote them in full, but I may merely say that they show that these producers are satisfied with the reduction both on crude and on refined.
Now, I wish to quote from a Liberal paper, but only as to what I take to be a statement of fact as to the opinion in the west. The Winnipeg ' Free Press ' says :
One of the tariff changes that will be most popular in the west is the cut in the coal oil duty. When the Liberals came into power they found this duty six 'cents a gallon. In their first revision they cut it to five cents per gallon and this has now been reduced to two and a half cents. The record gives ground for hoping that ultimately the whole duty will go and coal oil
will be free	The new duty came into
effect on Wednesday. To-day the wholesale price of oil is 2J cents per gallon less than It was on Wednesday. The whole benefit of the reduction will be enjoyed by the consumer.
In another item the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' has the following :
Immediately upon receipt of the information the Imperial Oil Company notified all its agents to put the selling price 2J cents a gallon less than it has been ; and the reduced rates went into immediate effect. The reduction applies to all grades of illuminating oils and naphtha. On the stocks already in hand, imported under the old duty, the company will lose by the reduction, but large shipments are coming in under the new rate.
The reduction will be greatly appreciated throughout the west, where the high price of coal oil has for years been a grievance.
While there are some who take a view the .very reverse of that which I hold, and who believe that the oil industry has received a blow from which it cannot recover, I believe I am divulging no secret when I say that hon. gentlemen In this House who have received letters and telegrams approving the change in the oil duties and congratulating the Liberal party upon it. find that those messages come signed by Conservatives as well as by Liberals.
It is not my purpose to deal at any very great length with the tariff. We on this side are charged with inconsistency because we do not follow out the radical ideas we held at one time. But it has been well said that the man who never changes his

views is likely to hold views that are very much in need of changing. In a practical world we must govern ourselves to some extent by the conditions as we find them. We may not be prepared to go as far as hon. gentlemen opposite are, but we are prepared to recognize the changes in conditions, and, in a practical way, to modify our policy to meet the circumstances of the country as they actually exist.
With the general tariff changes, I have no fault to find. If the argument advanced by our friends opposite is a good argument that with increased duties, competition among the manufacturers will keep down prices of manufactured articles there is no reason to fear increased prices as far as woollens and other manufactured articles are concerned. If the manufacturers do not enter into combines I believe the people will derive benefit ip connection therewith. I am not one of those who believe in the spirit of retaliation. I do not believe in erecting a tariff wall against our American friends simply because they have a tariff against us. Being contiguous to the United States we must trade with them and the best policy we can pursue is one of maintaining amicable relations as far as it is possible to -do so. I admit that I do not like the) spirit manifested by our American friends. I do not like the spirit of tariff hostility that they have frequently displayed towards us, but I do not know that it would be wise to raise our tariff as high as theirs, although in the nature of things there may be and I dare say there will be a general revision of the tariff which will perhaps place us in a more equitable position than that which we occupy at the present time. It seems to me that the government have dealt with a serious situation in so far as the dumping clause is concerned. How that will work out and how it may prove by experience, I am not prepared to say. I anticipate that it will prove to be an obstacle greater than anything we have at the present time in the way of the undue and unfair slaughtering of goods which has been carried on by our American friends. But. I would like to see our own Canadian people manifesting a greater spirit of selfdependence than we have displayed up to the present time. I think, that, with our national resources and with our circumstances as favourable as they are, we should endeavour by self-assertion and independence to control our own markets without depending so much on paternal assistance or aid.
There are one or two points not specially dealt with in connection with the tariff that I want to allude to. They are perhaps the outcome of our system. Reference was made the other evening to the question of immigration. ' One of the speakers on the other side of the House with a swing
of his arm and a good deal of force in his manner said that he did not think we ought to encourage immigrants to come here from the slums of Europe. I agree with him entirely but I think we have very little reason to find fault, as far as the immigrants which we are receiving are concerned. It is well known, and if it is not well, known it ought to be, that the government make no special arrangement as far as immigrants are concerned except to look after immigrants and do what they can to secure them by legitimate means. No assistance is offered to immigrants and as far as undesirable immigrants are concerned I do not think we have a great deal to fear ip that respect. I well remember that when the Mennonites came into the Northwest Territories as settlers some of our friends of the opposition offered very strong objections against them. They were said to be an undesirable class. It was saidi that they ditfered from our own people in their habits of life, and in their religion. It was said that they had certain peculiarities which our people did not approve of. But I believe that our hon. friends on the other side of the House will now admit that the Mennonites are among the best settlers we have in the Northwest. The Mennonite settlers are the wealthiest in that western country. Objection has been taken to the Doukliobors and Galicians on the score that they are undesirable settlers. I am quite free to say that the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is himself a convert to the view that the Galicians are a desirable class of settlers. I do not know that he has ever taken exception to them but' there have been hon. members on the other side of the House who seemed, fo think that it was not advisable to allow these immigrants to come into our territory. What are the facts as far as the Douk-hobors are concerned ? I am told by those who reside in the neighbourhood of the Doukhobors that a Doukhobor's word is as good as his bond, that if he goes into a store and asks for credit promising to pay for his goods at a specified time in the future the merchant will give him the credit which he desires and he will meet his engagements on the very day that he promises to do so. I find on looking into their transactions that when they require any article for their use they buy, for instance, ploughs by the hundred, overalls by the thousand, and sugar by five carload lots, I find that notwithstanding their peculiar views and religion they are assimilating themselves very rapidly with our own peo-pel, and I believe that within a very short time they will be a very desirable class of settlers indeed. When we take the figures showing the number of settlers who have come in during the last year I do not think we have very much ground to fear as far
I don't know.

Well, I do know, and whether the hon. gentleman knows it or not, I know further that whenever the estimates come up for consideration, my hon. friend who interjects the remark, and others of his friends with him, have asked for increased expenditure.
I would like the hon. member to name a single item that I asked for.

It is not easy for me off hand to mention a particular item that the hon. gentleman has asked for, but I am within the judgment of this House in saying, that he as well as other members of the opposition have asked for increased expenditure when the estimates were under consideration. If he has not so asked, he is an exception on the other side of the House, and I accept his apology. Now, Mr. Speaker, we spent $500,009 more on lighthouse and ocean service, than was spent in 1896.
I suppose our friends on the other side will; admit that this money was not improperly spent. Indeed the Conservative press are contending now, in view of the lamentable ' accident which occurred the other day, that we should spend, more money on this service so as to improve our navigation system. We spent $100,000 more on the fisheries service, and about $500,000 more on immigration than we did in 1896, and lam sure my hon. friends opposite will not object to that expenditure. We spent $332,000 more on the customs service than we did in 1896, but against that we collected $17,170,000 more in customs revenue. We spent $8.000 more on excise service than we did in 1896, but our revenue from this source increased by $4,000,000. We spent on postal service for the benefit of the people of Canada $400,000 more than we did in 1896 but the revenue from our postal service has increased by nearly $1,500,000. Let me digress for a moment at this point. I wish to call attention to the exceptionally favourable condition of our postal service under the able administration of the present Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock). The business people of the country admit, and the people of Canada generally admits that we have at the present day the best postal service we ever had in the history of the Dominion. We not only have had a saving of one-third on our domestic postage, but we have had a saving of one-third on our foreign postage. I well remember when Sir William Mulock proposed to reduce the rate of postage, member after member on the Conservative side of the House got up in their places and predicted it would be necessary to put a special tax upon tea or upon sugar, in order to make up the deficit they thought would follow7 the reduction of the postal rate. They could hardly be blamed for this, in view7 of the fact under Conservative rule w7e had a deficit of $700,-

000 or $800,000 annually In the Post Office Department, notwithstanding that we also had a three cent rate of postage. To the credit of the present Postmaster General, be it said, that it was not only unnecessary to put a special tax upon any article of consumption, but that be has been able to give us increased facilities all over this Dominion, and in addition to that he has turned the old annual deficit of Conservative days, into a surplus. The people of this broad Dominion appreciate the fact that they are now reaping advantages and benefits in the post office service to which they were strangers before the Liberals came into power. It is true that the expenses of the Intercolonial Railway have increased over $5,000,000, but every dollar of that has come back to the people of this country.
Now Mr. Speaker, I have given a brielf review of the expenditure made by this government, and in conclusion permit me to say that the prosperous state of the country, as revealed through the budget speech, is sufficient to justify the warmest eulogy of this government. Some of our Conerva-, five friends say : that the government are entitled to no credit for the existing prosperity, but the member for South Wentworth (Mr. E. D. Smith) was frank enough to admit that government was responsible to a certain extent for prosperity or for depression. No less an authority than the Toronto ' Mail,' commenting on the budget speech delivered in 1882, said :
Instead of bringing the country to the brink of insolvency, the present government has caused evbry vein to quiver with healthy activity.
If that be true, what language could be more suitably applied to the present government ? What government ever in Canada before has caused every vein to pulsate with healthy activity ? Our friends on the other side of the House have endeavoured as far as they can, to minimize the credit that should accrue, and has accrued, to the government because of their wise administration of public affairs, but the people of Canada know better, and I have not the slightest doubt that they will pay their tribute of confidence in this Liberal government in the days to come. The prosperous state of the country, as revealed in the budget speech, must commend itself to both Liberals and Conservatives who look upon the question from an impartial standpoint. There are Conservatives who are willing to admit, that Canada now enjoys a higher state of prosperity than ever before ; there are Conservatives who are candid enough to say, at least in private conversation, that thisi government has been a good administration ; there are Conservatives who are frank enough to acknowledge that the administration of this government has been superior to that which preceded it. And, Sir, whether these Conservatives are will- I

ing to vote for the government or not, it makes no difference so long as in their heart of hearts they give the credit to this government for its wise acts of public policy. The good times have been shared in by all ; by the farmer, by the manufacturer, by the artisan, by the invester; and the record of the government as portrayed in the budget speech is one on which the government can confidently appeal for the approval of the country. I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that be the day near or be it far, when it shall be necessary to appeal to the electorate for the endorsation of the policy of this government, the far-seeing, hard headed, thoughtful electors of the Dominion, will show their appreciation of a governrfient whose policy has worked to the best interests of all classes of the community. We on this side of the House claim with pride, that this government is the best government Canada has ever known. We make that claim in view of the facts which have been disclosed ; we claim it in view of the record of the government which stands without parallel in the history of the world, and which record has been ably presented to the country by the Minister of Finance in his bud-.get speech.

Mr. Speaker, the remarks of my hon. friend from West Huron (Mr. Holmes) are for the most part of a very general character, and I think they have already been pretty well answered by hon. gentlemen who have spoken. I do not propose to speak at any great length, and therefore my hon. friend (Mr. Holmes) will excuse me if I fail to follow him through all the phases of his eloquent speech.
Perhaps just a passing word might be given to the eloquent peroration with which he concluded. I do not quite remember whether he described this government as the best government this country ever possessed or the best government the world ever possessed-some hon. gentleman on that side of the House go that far occasionally. He claimed for it, that it had caused the veins of the country to pulsate with a splendid activity. Well, he was altogether too modest. Why did he not claim that it had caused the veins of the whole commercial world to pulsate with a splendid activity ? He has as much justification for the one contention as for the other. But I observe that my hon. friend, like a great many others who address the House on this question, fails absolutely on every occasiou to point to one single measure introduced and carried out by his administration to which the prosperity of this country is in any way due. That is the difficult aspect of the question from their standpoint. It is all very well to claim for Canada prosperity. We know we have it; we know also that we have had prosperity all through the

world ; and unless we can attribute the prosperity which prevails in Canada to some act of the present administration, are we not forced to agree with an hon. gentleman whose authority my hon. friend from West Huron will not dispute, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), who said that the prosperity which Canada in common with the rest of the world has enjoyed during the past eight years is due to causes over which governments have no control whatever.
Having said so much, I shall now refer to the speech with which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) introduced his budget. Although that speech contains some rather noteworthy statements, I may be permitted to draw attention to the fact that it was perhaps as remarkable for its omissions as for what.it actually contained. The hon. Minister of Finance, as was pointed out by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell), made no estimate whatever of the revenue or the expenditure for the coming year. In that respect he departed from the course which he and all the other Ministers of Finance have followed on previous occasions. Not only did he make no reference to the revenue or the expenditure for the coming year, but he gave the House not the slightest explanation of that remarkable omission. Let me point to another omission in the speech of the hon. gentleman. One would have supposed that the Minister of Finance, speaking on a matter not only of political import, but of business importance to the whole country, would have been disposed to give to the people a fair and accurate statement of our affairs, and not to confine himself solely to those aspects of the business and the finances of the country which might be of use to his party in the distribution of campaign literature. The hon. gentleman went over a period of years with regard to our trade returns, but he made not one reference to the increase of taxation or the increase of expenditure. My hon friend dealt generally with the increase of trade in this country during the past eight years, but he made not one reference to a subject on which the hon. gentleman who sits beside him (Sir Bichard Cartwright) has dilated at great length in days gone by-the relative trade of this country with the United States as compared with its trade with Great Britain. Not one word out of the niouth of the Minister of Finance ; and stranger still, not one word out of the mouth of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who used to continually harp on that matter in days gone by. That indicates that these hon. gentlemen were not giving fair candid statements with reference to the business of this country, but were making campaign speeches for distribution throughout the country, and therefore saw fit to omit from their remarks every possible aspect of our
present conditions which might in any way call for criticism from gentlemen in this House or from business men throughout the country as a whole.
Now, it will be necessary for me to lay before the House some statements, which I will do very briefly, to remedy the omissions from the speech of the hon. Minister of Finance. Let me say, in the first place, that I do not object to a reasonable expenditure in this country. We could hot reasonably expect that from . 1896 to the present time there would not be some increase of expenditure in a rapidly-growing country such as this. The point we have taken in this House is that expenditure, especially on public works, should be conducted on some systematic basis, and should not be made the means of distributing favours to partisans, and should not be regulated solely by partisan considerations. We are glad to see money expended in this country, and we expect that our expenditure shall reasonably increase ; but let us bear in mind that we have been warned by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce that matters shall not always be in this country as they are today. It was only a day or two ago that the Minister of Trade and Commerce uttered a last warning on that point-a warning which had been given to this country many times before by the Minister of Finance. Now, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) dwelt on the question of preferential trade. He says that the attitude of the two parties in Canada is practically the same on that question. X am glad to hear my hon. friend the Minister of Finance make that statement. The agreement must have come about very speedily, if it has come about at all. The policy of the Conservative party was set forth by a resolution in this House. I do not recollect that hon. gentlemen on the other side were prepared to support the policy which we then declared. But I want to tell them, speaking with whatever authority I may possess, that the Conservative party has not changed its policy on this point since 1899, when a resolution, proposed by Sir Charles Tupper was voted down by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. If there has been a change it is on the other side, not on this, because we are prepared to stand by the words of the resolution now as we did then. The words of the resolution are these :
This House is of opinion that a system of mutual trade preference between Great Britain and Ireland and the colonies would greatly stimulate increased production in and commerce between these countries and would thus promote and maintain the unity of the empire, and that nothing which falls short of the complete realization of such a policy should he considered as final or satisfactory.
Therefore, if the Minister of Finance says that the parties are at one in regard to the question at the present time, it means that these hon. gentlemen are doing in policy Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
what, I trust, they will very soon do otherwise-cross from that side of the House to this. What was the attitude of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) himself long after we proclaimed that policy. Why, his contention in 1901 and 1902 was that it would be absolutely absurd to expect any system of preferential trade with the mother country unless we adopted free trade and did away with our tariff altogether. I have the right hon. gentleman's words under my hand, but, unless he contradicts what I have said, I will not weary the House with them for I have already too many quotations in this speech. And what was the attitude of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in those days. His attitude was that any effort to be made by Sir Charles Tupper along the lines he had suggested-that is, any effort to obtain a preference in the mother country in return for a preference given to the mother country -was arrant humbug ; and he went further and characterized as arrant humbug resolutions of boards of trade throughout the country urging upon the government to make efforts in that direction with the least possible delay. The two parties stand on the same platform now, do they 7 Well, I have some recollection that my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) when he was in Great Britain did not stand on the same platform or advocate the same policy as that announced by the Minister of Finance this year, and announced with even greater emphasis by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech of last year. What did my right hon. friend say when he was in Great Britain, after he had secured the return to office of his party in this country pledged to do whatever he could to obtain a preference for the products of Canada in the mother country ? He went to the mother country and told the people and statesmen of Great Britain that we wanted no preference in their makets for our products. But only last year, and previously at the Colonial Conference, we were treated to a series of threats by these gentlemen directed against the mother country, that the preference we had granted in 1897 would be withdrawn unless a similar preference were granted to the products of Canada by the mother country. The people of Great Britain were told in 1897-were they not ?-that Canada had not granted the preference which was then given to the mother country with any hope, or, indeed with any desire, of obtaining anything in return. It was given-said my right hon. friend-' in return for the splendid freedom with which you have endowed us. ' And further he said-and this is especially to be noted-we do not want any preference in return, because we do not wish to see the mother country cursed by that protection which has wrought so much of evil in Canada. My right hon. friend will not deny, and has never denied that utter-

ance. The published reports of his speeches contain these words, and I have them under my hand, if he should see fit to deny them. Why should we now demand a preference in return if we had already received compensation for the preference we gave ? Why do we now desire to see the mother country cursed by that protection which has destroyed Canada in the view of my right hon. friend ? !Why ido we make these threats against the mother country ? My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, in his speech of this year-and I have a number of quotations from his speech of last year, with which I shall not weary the House- says :
For the present we think it is a wise policy to adhere to the preferential system in the hope that it may be adopted more generally throughout the empire and that by and by a better understanding may be come to in the mother country and that it will be adopted there as well.
But no one understood that to be the policy of this government up to 18 months ago because the language of the Prime Minister in 1897 was followed by words of the Minister of Agriculture in two or three speeches in Great Britain in 1901 in which, speaking with all the responsibility of a Minister of the Crown, he again repeated to the British people that no preference was desired by Canada because the preference which we had given was accorded to the mother country for altogether different reasons and upon an altogether different principle. When the Chancellor of the Exchequer was asked in the parliament of Great Britain : ' Do you propose to exempt Canada from the tax on food products ? ' he replied :
' No. X do not propose to exempt Canada from this tax because Canada desires no such exemption.' Does my right hon. friend now desire to see the mother country cursed by protection ? Does he stand for and believe in Mr. Chamberlain's policy ? I am sorry that if he has repented, his repentance has come so late because I venture to say that if the government of this country had expended as much time and effort in procuring a reciprocity treaty with Great Britain^-because that is all it amounts to-as they have expended in endeavouring to obtain reciprocal trade relations on fair terms with the United States, we would have had preferential trade on a fair basis and we would have had that preference in the markets of the mother country which would have done so much not only for the east but for the west of Canada and which would have poured population into this country in even greater numbers thau we have beheld with so much satisfaction during the past three or four years.
The terror of imperialism in invoked whenever this question is raised. Well, I would like to know what greater danger we run
by making a reciprocity treaty with the mother country, which is not a foreign country, than by making a reciprocity treaty with the United States of America ? What greater dangers are there in making a reciprocity treaty with Great Britain and Ireland than in making a reciprocity treaty with the United States of America ? Gentlemen who are very much alarmed at the prospect of reciprocity with the mother country were not afraid to take part in the deliberations of the commission which sat at Washington. Is there any greater danger in one case than in the other ? I would like to know what the danger is.
Let us look at it in another aspect. We have given a preference to the mother country. Do we run any greater danger of imperialism by receiving a preference in return ? Where does the danger come in ? I have endeavoured to concern myself with this a little as I propose to stand as strongly and as firmly as any one for all those liberties which we enjoy in Canada, and especially for the right of self government in Canada, which we shall never give up. But I do not understand why we run more risk in the one case than in the other, and I do not understand that we incur any risk at all, having given a preference to the mother country, by merely receiving one in return. When any government in Great Britain proposes to give to us a preference in their markets upon terms which are inconsistent with our rights of self-government we shall know very well, on this side of the House at least, what answer to give and we will say that no advantage of that kind would for one moment be considered if it involved the least diminution of those rights of self-government which we have enjoyed for so many years and have won by so much effort and at so great a cost.	That is my position
and I believe it is the position of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. Then we are told that this government dare not interfere, dare not announce any policy on the subject, dare not become a party to any resolution because, forsooth, this has become a party question in the mother country and it would be impolitic to express our opinion. Well we have not always been so careful in the past. We interfered for example in connection with the war in South Africa by passing a resolution in this House, yet, I think that there was somewhat of a party question in the mother country even at that time. When will this cease to be a party question in Great Britain ? Suppose that Mr. Chamberlain's project carries eventually and he comes into power and is prepared to negotiate with Canada ; does any one suppose that the free traders of Great Britain will be absolutely eliminated, or that this will not continue to be a party question in the mother country ? Is it the policy of the

government that we shall sit still and fold our hands until the last sole survivor of the Cobden club has passed away ? If not, it seems to me we are a little too careful in Canada at the present time and that we might well in this country state at least our willingness to enter into negotiations for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not some fair basis of mutual preferential trade cannot be obtained. I have always thought that when the principle was once adopted by the statesmen of the two countries it would be largely a matter for the business men of the two countries to work out. I believe it could be worked out and worked out with advantage to the mother country as well as to Canada herself.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) contends that Canada led the way in preferential trade. We know how Canada led the way. She led the way because there were two warring factions in the cabinet and a system of preferences to the mother country was agreed upon as a compromise between these two factions; and we know that the leader of one of the factions, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, stated distinctly and emphatically when he spoke upon the subject in 1897 that he agreed to it because it was some installment of free trade and because the ship's head was now at last pointed towards the open sea of free trade. Now that same lion, gentleman will stand up in the House and vote, if a vote should be taken, in favour of an increase in the woollen duties that takes away 60 per cent of the preference upon those articles and he will rejoice no doubt to see in that regard the ship's head pointed in exactly the opposite direction.
I do not know that I need discuss the attitude of the hon. gentleman very much, particularly in his absence to-day, but I am almost inclined to think that his views upon that question or any other question will not be very highly regarded by very many of his fellow countrymen until he can give some better explanation than his leader has given of his attitude between 1878 and 1896 as compared with his attitude from 1896 to the present time. We have an explanation from the right hon. gentleman of the attitude of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce from 1878 to 1896 and I am bound to say that if the remarks of the right hon. Prime Minister on that occasion were intended as a eulogy of Sir Richard Cartwright it was the most cruel eulogy that one friend ever pronounced upon another.
I spoke of omissions from the speech of the hon. Minister of Finance. He said not one word about the conditions of our import trade with Great Britain as compared Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
with our import trade with the United States. This was a favourite text in days gone by. How does the matter stand today ? One thing that ought to be remembered is that if we take the $66,000,000 balance of trade in our favour with Great Britain and add $13,000,000 of our own money, the product of our resources in Canada, we are just able to make up the $79,000,000 which we have to pay to the United States. How does it come about that with the British preference the relative conditions of trade between this country and the United States as compared with those between this country and the mother country as so extraordinary as I have pointed out ? Of course, one realizes that the mother country is our

customer. The United States can never be our customer in respect to many of our products. The United States is our rival in the markets of Great Britain and it is for that reason that I for one am prepared to support proposals for a reciprocity treaty with Great Britain rather than for a reciprocity treaty with the United States pf America. The people of the United States are our commercial rivals; the British people afford us our market, and I suppose it will continue in future that our exports to the mother country will be greater than our imports from the mother country.
Bet us look for one moment at the rate of duty. The rate of duty upon dutiable goods imported from the United States during the past year was 24-91 ; the rate of duty upon dutiable goods imported from the mother country was 23:32 : the rate of duty on all goods, dutiable and free, from the United States during the past year was 13-25 ; while the rate of duty upon all goods imported from Great Britain was considerably higher, being no less than 16-71 ; showing to what extent the United States has the advantage over the mother country in respect to free goods at least. Let us remember that both with respect to the trade from Great Britain and with respect to the rate of duty, there will probably be a still greater change in favour of the United States, in view of the proposed alterations in the tariff. I do not wish for one moment to be understood as not standing for protection to the woollen industry of Canada, but I do not forget that when this preference was given to the mother country, the duty upon many articles which we especially import from the mother country was raised, while the duty upon some at least which we import largely from the United States was correspondingly lowered.
I shall consider the tariff proposals of the government only briefly now. because they will more properly be discussed in committee. They are described by the government press in certain quarters, as being in the direction of higher protection, while in other quarters the idea of increased protection is discounted, and attention is called solely to certain reductions. It is interesting to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance drawn as willing captives in the train of the so-called robber barons who were described in such terms of opprobrium in days gone by by the member for South Oxford (Sir Richard Cartwright). If the government is adopting any measure of higher protection, let us remember that according to the right hon gentleman (Sir Richard Cartwright) the government is embarking upon an orgy of the most awful corruption, because it is not long since he said :
I do not mean to say that a government may not be corrupt and yet not protectionist. That '

may be. But I do say that human nature being as it is, it is almost impossible for a government to be protectionist and escape being corrupt.
And I will add this further ; I will add that while I think protection and corruption are practically inseparable ; I will add that I likewise believe for my part, that protection and true freedom are all but absolutely incompatible.
According to the view of the right hon. gentleman, then, this government is plunging into a career not only of wild corruption, but into a career which will land the country in an absolute condition of slavery. I have before quoted the remarks .of the Prime Minister on this question and I need not quote them again. Sufficient it is to say that the Prime Minister, only two years before he came into power, denounced protection as absolute slavery and robbery and he has since prided himself that having begun life as a protectionist he is now a free trader. Be that as it may, a more recent utterance of the Prime Minister in Montreal, informed us that he is now neither a protectionist nor a free trader, but a practical man. Let me remind the right hon. gentleman that almost the last public utterance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce upon this question, before 1896 was in moving a resolution in 1895, when he said :
I doubt if there ever was a country so wholly and utterly unsuited to protection as a country like Canada.
Might we be permitted to inquire whether he still adheres to that view so honestly and firmly pronounced. No one has questioned the honesty of his former utterances except his leader.
If inquiry into the tariff be necessary before revision takes place one would have supposed that such inquiry would be required as to certain matters that are dealt with in the tariff, notably the oil industry, which, as I understand it, presents a pretty complicated question for consideration. But the pretense of a necessity for inquiry was not always put forward by the government. In 1901 those who desired to revise the tariff were told by the government that the Joint High Commission was sitting ; in 1902 the excuse of the government was that the Colonial Conference was about to take place, and in 1903 the excuse was that until we learned the exact outcome of Mr. Chamberlain's agitation for a system of mutual preferential trade within the empire, it would be unwise to interfere with the tariff. But this year, there being no other excuse available for the government, we are told that these ministers who have been collecting information on this subject for the last four years, must have an inquiry. Have they not technical officers in their departments ? Have they not received delegations from the manufacturing, the agricultural, the lumbering, the

mining, and indeed all industries in Canada ? Have they not had an enormous mass of information placed at their disposal, and why is it that they shirk from making a tariff revision this session ? That question will present itself to every thoughtful man in the country.
In connection with the oil duties, the Minister of Finance presents a very charming picture by which the people will be saved $643,886 per annum upon the oil duties, while they pay a bounty of nearly $225,000. That is a very excellent condition of affairs, if the government could have any assurance' that under existing and probably future conditions, the reduction in the price of oil will correspond with the reduction in the duty. When we get into committee I would like to hear some explanations from the Minister of Finance on that point before I would be prepared to join in his felicitations to himself on making that change in the tariff. There are various interests to be reckoned with in this connection. There is the oil refining industry which must not be lost sight of by any means, because it affords remunerative employment to many Canadians. There is the producer of crude oil to be considered, and his interests are very important.
I would not at first blush, and without hearing something further from my hon. friend the Minister of Finance than I have been able to hear so far, be inclined to agree with him that the interests of those producers are so thoroughly safeguarded by the proposed bounty as he seems to imagine. Is this bounty to be permanent ? Bounties are not usually provided with the intention that they are to be permanent. What is the view of the government on that point ? How is this difficult situation to be adjusted ?-because we must endeavour as far as possible to do justice to all. How is it that under conditions of that kind the government were able to spring to a conclusion without any difficulty whatever, whereas with regard to a great many other industries of Canada, the conditions of which are not of so complicated a character the government have found it absolutely necessary to postpone their decision ? One would like to understand something of the reasons why very difficult and complicated conditions were met promptly in the one case, and why less difficult and less complicated conditions in other cases receive 110 amelioration without a certain inquiry. These are considerations to which we cannot shut our eyes, and as to which we shall exact certain information from the government when we come to discuss this matter in committee.
With regard to the increased duty on woollens, I speak with all the diffidence of one who has not the experience possi-essed by a great many other gentlemen in this House. I have not had. an opportunity
of consulting very much those familiar with the conditions of the woollen industry; but, speaking from what I know on the subject and simply from the standpoint of common sense, I would have thought that the importation of shoddy would have been better met by a specific duty. I think that the importation of what is called shoddy ought especially to he dealt with, because not only is it destructive of the interests of our manufacturers, but it seems to present unfortunate conditions from the standpoint of the purchaser, consisting as it does of goods which look well, but which do not wear well, and in the end do not give that value to the purchaser which he has a right to expect in consideration of the money he pays for them. However, we shall have further opportunity of discussing that question when we get into committee.
As to the provision against dumping, this I am sure, must have been enthusiastically heralded by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce. 1 was very much struck with certain observations which he made on that subject two years ago, and I was especially struck with an article in the leading organ of the .Liberal party in the province of Ontario, the Toronto ' Globe,' on this very subject only last autumn. The argument presented by the Toronto ' Globe ' was this : Far from dumping being any disadvantage to the people of Canada, it was the very thing the people of Canada wanted. How, asked this great organ of public opinion, can it be of any disadvantage to Canadians to buy for $1.00 goods worth $1.50? Shall we -exhort our fellow countrymen to refrain from purchasing them ? The trend of the argument was that if there was one thing above another that we should welcome in Canada, it would be the wholesale importation of manufactured goods from the United States to be sold in Canada for one-half of what they could be purchased for in this country. I went through a great jrart of the maritime provinces, into the eastern townships of the province of Quebec, and into the western part of the province of Ontario, and I pointed out to the people whom I addressed from every platform,, that dumping, as I believed, was a very serious evil. I said to them :	When the
Canadian industry has been wiped -out;, when the Canadian factory has been closed, when the Canadian employee has been driven to seek his home in the United States of America and to work in those very factories which are sending these goods into Canada, and when you come to add up the account, even then, with the dumping of goods at reduced prices, I believe you would find the account against this country ; but add to that consideration the fact that when our factories have been once closed, and the employees driven to

a foreign country, you will find these trusts closing their hands, and compelling the people to pay 50 per cent more than the value of the goods; then make up the account and see where this country will be in the long run. I was not heralded by any Liberal newspaper as setting forth sound doctrine. My arguments were ridiculed; and yet when the Minister of Finance utters practically the same doctrine only the other day in the budget speech, he is heralded as the proclaimer of glad tidings by every Liberal journal throughout the country. That shows to what extent partisan politics will drive us.
Let us see what my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce thinks of his question of dumping; and I commend his remarks especially to the Prime Minister, because we all know . that that right hon. gentleman put forward the present Minister of Trade and Commerce as the great exponent of the fiscal policy of the Liberal party in days gone (by. Surely nothing has occurred since which would cause him to lose confidence in the well weighed utterances of that hon. gentleman. I will not put this statement forward as the utterance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce merely. I have a right to put it forward as the deliberate utterance of this government through the Minister of Trade and Commerce on this very question only two years ago; and T will let my right hon. friend repudiate it, if he sees fit to do so, as the deliberate utterance of the government of which he is the head. Here is a statement of the views of the government on the question of dumping :
I have heard it said by hon. gentlemen opposite, and even by some friends of mine, that Canada is a dumping ground for American manufacturers. I have heard plaintive wails that heathen Yankees, not having the fear ct God or of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association before their eyes, come to Canada and actually have the audacity to sell goods to Canadian consumers at a lower price than that at which they sell them to their own people.
Whose views are those, please ?

These are the views of the government as pronounced by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce less than two years ago. That was In the finest vein of sarcasm of the hon. gentjleman'; and he continued as follows.
It is even said, though this lacks proof, that they sell them at less than 'cost in their greed to monopolize so profitable a trade ; and it is said that there are many Canadians so unpatriotic, so dead to all lofty feeling, that they will actually purchase American goods for no better reason than the fact that they can obtain them better and cheaper than they can similar goods in their own country.
That was the sympathetic way in which the government only two years ago treated Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
the complaint by the producers and manufacturers of this country that they were suffering from the dumping of American goods. Once more we have a right about face by tbe administration and we welcome it if the measures taken to cure the evil will only prove effective, but I believe the government are taking these measures in a very half-hearted way and that they will not prove effective. We will have some opportunity no doubt hereafter to consider the reasons which lead us to that conclusion. My right hon. friend seems to be touched with the merry spirit of this utterance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I do not know which portion of it has excited his risibility.

speechtext: The comments of my hon. friend.

I was endeavouring to be a little humourous and am glad that I hit the mark. Well, we. are to have a very curious system, very curious measures to remove this evil, and very effective no doubt my right hon. friend thinks.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I hope so.

I suppose those hopes will be realized just as was the expectation of my right hon. friend that he would absolutely destroy protection when he came to office or that he would reduce our expenditure by $4,000,000. Does my right hon. friend think these hopes will materialize any better than did his splendid prophecy at Toronto with regard to the fast Atlantic ocean service ? He only hopes now but then he had a certainty. Then he produced a telegram. At present, however, we are not on very safe ground. Then we had an assurance and a certainty, but now we have only a hope. What then is likely to result since our expectation now must be so faint as compared with that which the good people of Toronto and all the good citizens of Canada were led to entertain at that time ? Goods have at present to he entered at their market value in the country they come from. The customs law requires that, and no change in that respect has been outlined by the Minister of Finance. The imposition of a special tax will turn therefore altogether upon the individual discretion of each customs officer, and we will have this extraordinary condition of things all over Canada. Importers will be met with one reception at Toronto, another at Montreal and another at Halifax, depending altogether on the judgment, vigilance, experience and knowledge of each customs officer. A thousand things which are uncertain will enter into the enforcement of this statute, and I venture to say that the expectations of my right hon. friend as to the effect of this measure will be found hardly up to the results even of his assurance with regard to the fast Atlantic service, because the expec-

tation in that ease was kept up at least two or three years, although it has absolutely faded away for the present. Cannot the increased duty be evaded by some system of annual discounts or some other such arrangement ? Men familiar with business life can inform the House better on that point than I can. Last but not least, the hon. gentleman's remedy will absolutely fail to operate when prices are generally depressed to an undue degree in other countries. When prices come down all over the United States, goods will be sold in Canada at what might be called dumping prices otherwise, but at the same prices as in the United States. Where will the protection be found then? The market may be so glutted at home that the American manufacturers will be compelled to send their goods to Canada at the prices ruling in the United States. We must not forget that the United States produced thirteen thousand million dollars worth of manufactured goods in 1901 and exported only three and a half per cent of that quantity. Let us consider for a moment what an enormous surplus they would have for export in a time of depression. If only ten per cent instead of three and a half per cent had to be marketed in some foreign country, that would mean an increase of exports to thirteen hundred and fifty million dollars. Where would those goods be dumped first? No doubt in Canada, which is the best customer of the United States for manufactured goods. I venture therefore to think that this provision will not prove a sufficient safeguard for Canadian interests. Further than that, if goods should be sold in the United States as low as fifty per cent of their value, the duty proposed would still enable them to be sold in this country at lower prices than they can be manufactured at in Canada. Canadian manufacturers cannot specialize their manufacture as the Americans can. We have only a home market of 6,000,000 as against a home market of 80,000,000 which the Americans enjoy. I have been astonished sometimes, on going through the industrial establishments
of our country, to observe the enormous number and variety of articles which men are compelled to manufacture in order to retain the Canadian market. I have not been able to understand how it is possible to turn out such an extraordinary variety of articles and carry on business with any profit ; but I have been told that unless they do turn out this almost infinite variety of articles, it is absolutely impossible for them to hold the market, because the dealers demand this large variety and if they cannot get it at home they will get it from the United States or Great Britain.
Another criticism which has been mentioned is one to which attention is directed by a very able man, Mr. William McMaster of Montreal. I am not sufficiently familiar with the tariff to know how much importance is to be attached to it, but I attach importance to it because Mr. McMaster has raised the point. He says :
' Our important point,' said Mr. McMaster,
' is what effect this will have on free trade. For instance, steel for many edged tools is admitted free. Would it he fair to allow a man importing free to get the advantage of slaughter prices, while others importing, say under a five per cent duty, would have to pay this additional charge ; it would really amount to a bonus on the free goods. No doubt these points will be settled ere long, but in the meantime I can certainly endorse the principle of the change.'
But Mr. McMaster is very careful not to endorse the means by which that change is to be carried out. The general conditions of trade call strongly for a tariff on fairly protective lines. I have a statement here of the principal dutiable imports from Great Britain and the United States and I will call attention to some of the figures. I shall not read the whole statement, as it would take up too much time-and I fear that I have already unduly trespassed on the time of the House-but I shall quote some of them. I realize that, with respect to some of these manufactured articles we cannot legitimately hope to have the whole Canadian market. But I do believe that with respect to many of these articles we should have full control of the Canadian market, or at least to a far greater extent than we have at the present time, Look at iron and steel manufactures, in which we increased our importation from Great Britain and the United States by more than $16,000,000 in the period which elapsed between 1896 and 1903. The tariff on iron and steel and manufactures of iron and steel has not been touched at all, except in so far as it may be modified by the proposed dumping provision in which I have not a great deal of confidence. One of our great iron industries, that in the province of Nova Scotia has been in more or less trouble. Another, that at the Soo is being re-orgauized. In respect of both industries, we have reason to believe that the government his been asked to give greater protection. I should think that in that respect, and in respect of many other articles which I have enumerated the interest of the country calls for a readjustment of the tariff upon a fair and reasonable basis having regard not so much to the interest of the manufacturers themselves-because I am not standing for their interest especially-but having regard to the interest of the whole country, the interest of the people who obtain employment in great manufacturing establishments. These, even more than the men whose capital is invested, are interested in seeing that these manufactures are put upon a thoroughly sound basis, a basis which will enable the men who have employed their resources in these industries to give to the labouring men a fair and reasonable wage.
