And the question for this parliament and for the Canadian people is whether or not the labour involved in the manufacture of a great many of these articles, a very large proportion of the total of that sum of fifty-two and a half million dollars might not have been given to our own people at a remunerative wage rather than to the people of other countries.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have detained the House very much longer than I expected to do when I began. Let me say, in order

to be brief, that I stand by the principles which I advocated last year as those upon which we should proceed in the re-adjustment of the tariff. And, for the purpose of being brief, I will read those principles instead of describing and elaborating them :
Our policy should be to accomplish the following object® :-
1.	To so arrange our tariff that all legitimate industries at present established in this country should be so protected as to insure as far as possible permanency under conditions of depression as well as in times of commercial expansion.
2.	To invite capital and attract labour to the establishment of other industries which the resources and raw material of our country amply justify.
3.	To preserve by means of an adequately protective tariff our own home market for our own people and to have the policy of the government so declared and understood.
Because that is the very basis of all investment for the purpose of expanding the industries of Canada.
4.	In framing our tariff to have regard solely to the interests of Canada which have been committed to our charge, although recognizing that in consulting our own interests we must not be unmindful of the tariffs raised against us by other countries.
5.	To so frame our fiscal policy that labour in Canada shall be paid a fair living wage, remembering always that our labouring classes and therefore our producers and manufacturers cannot be expected to compete on even terms with countries in which the condition of life among the labouring classes is altogether different. We do not desire to reduce our labouring population to the low standard of living, to that-hard fierce struggle for existence which prevails in many countries. We do not want our labouring classes to compete without protection against the pauper labour of any country.
6.	To utilize the labour of our own people in the conversion of our own raw material into finished products required for use in our own country. It is surely bad policy to export our raw material, to send our labouring classes abroad to another country to find work in its manufactories and to send after both our money to pay for the finished product which we require.
And I say that not only the labouring men of Canada, not only the manufacturers of Canada, not only those who have capital invested and those who receive a wage out of the investment of capital, but the farmers of our country as well are intensely interested in seeing that we have a stable policy of protection carried out. The people of Canada are beginning to realize, the farmers I think are beginning to realize the value to them of the home market and of important industrial centres, of which we have few in this country to-day. Farmers, newly arrived farmers in the Northwest, pointed out to me a year and a half ago that in making their homes in Canada they felt the disadvantage of not having in western Canada those great industrial centres and centres of population that afforded them a market in the United States. That condition would come to us in the west of Canada, as well as in the east, if we had in force a policy such as I suggest, and such as we on this side of the House have fought for. Winnipeg and other great points in the west would become manufacturing centres, great industrial centres, before many years had passed, if we had in Canada a tariff adequately and firmly protective of our home market. And, Sir, with a policy such as I have outlined and with a thoroughly national system of transportation, whereby the people shall own and control the national highways, constructed by means of the national credit and out of the national resources, the development of this country will proceed on sure lines, on a stable basis and in a legitimate direction, and we shail have no cause to fear for the future material prosperity of the country which we love so well.
1 therefore beg to move :
That all the words after ' that ' in the proposed motion he left out and the following substituted therefor :
No readjustment of the tariff can be regarded as satisfactory which does not provide such protection to our labour, agricultural products, manufactures and industries as will secure the Canadian market for the Canadian people.
That at the present session there should he a thorough adjustment of the tariff based on a declared and stable policy of adequate protection. '

Mr. Speaker, I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) will be the first to admit that the speech which we have heard to-day from his lips is a very old friend. At all events, it is an old friend of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House ; it Is on this side of the House an old acquaintance. We have heard it before, and we have heard it during the present session even, from the lips of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell). I shall not say we have heard it too often ; quite the contrary, because if, after all, the policy of my hon. friends on the other side of the House is confined within the four corners of that speech, and if, as time goes on, and year after year rolls -upon us, we have the same thing over and over again, then after all we on this side of the House should be comforted with the thought that there is not much to find fault with in our policy. My hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) has dilated at some length on the question of figures. He has reproached us once more upon the fact that we have increased the expenditure. I do not know that it requires any justification on my part, or if I should endeavour to make a justification, that much labour would be required for that purpose, because I think that the expenditure which we have incurred has been amply justified, not only by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, hut even by hon. gentlemen on
r

[DOT] the other side. I would like to know, Sir, during the years we have been in office what items of the expenditure which have been proposed by this government have been opposed by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House ? The truth is that we are not sufficiently extravagant in the eyes of hon. gentlemen opposite, because again and again we hear them proposing to us to increase the expenditures which we have brought to the attention of the country. I have not time to go over these, but if I had time I am sure I could recall many instances in which hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have asked us to supplement estimates which we were bringing before the House and to vote more money than we were providing for. The chief object of my hon. friend's criticism has been the question of surpluses. My hon. friend, I may tell him again, is a good hand-not yet equal to Sir Charles Tupper, I admit-but not a bad hand at a scrap-book. He has quoted some sentences from speeches of my hon. friend (Sir Richard Cartwright) to the effect that the Minister of Finance had no need of having surpluses. Sir, I do not think if the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) were here he would have anything to recant, to apologize for or to explain on this subject. X have to say to my hon. friend that in such a new country as this a large amount of public money must be expended. We have to build railways, to build wharfs, to improve the canals and this involves a large expenditure. In the eight years we have been in office we have spent no less than $56,000,000 on capital expenditure providing for the construction of railways in different parts of the country and for the improvement of the canals, and I may say that at this time the country is the wealthier for the expenditure which we have made in that direction. Not only have we made the country all the wealthier for the expenditure which we have made, but 1 venture to say we should perhaps have spent a little more. We have been able to expend no less than $56,000,000 in that way on improvements which have added to the wealth of the people, and have been able to do this without adding one dollar to the public debt of this country.
There is our justification and I ask my hon. friend what are we to do 1 We have carried on this work with our surpluses. It is because my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), year after year has been able to make a record as that which he has made, it is because, year after year he has been able to have surpluses amounting to this large sum of money that we have been able to add to the wealth of the people of Canada without adding one cent to the public debt. If we had followed the suggestion of my hon. friend, if indeed it was a suggestion, or if we had done what his words imply, we would have taken means to reform the tariff in such a way Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
that instead of having this surplus to carry on these public works we would have been obliged borrow the money in the markets of the world. Is that the policy of my hon. friend ? If the argument advanced by my hon. friend this afternoon means anything it means that my hon. friend objects to the policy we have pursued. If it means anything it means that instead of carrying on these public works and of meeting these expenditures out of the money which we have placed in the public treasury he would have done the same thing by borrowing the money in the markets of the world. It means that instead of carrying on the public works of the country without putting any greater burden on the shoulders of the people, and without adding to the public debt we should have borrowed the money. If that is the position which my hon. friend takes I am willing to take issue with him. I am not only willing to take issue with him in this House, but am willing to allow that issue to be placed before the Canadian people. My hon. friend a moment ago rather stated that we would change sides in this House; he rather intimated that when the general elections came on in this country he and his friends would come to this side of the House and we would go to the other side of the House.
So you will.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have heard that before. I heard that in 1900 and it is a promise which has not yet been fulfilled. I am not strong in the line of prophecy but if my hon. friend wants to come into power it will not be by suggesting that in order to carry on the public works we should borrow the money instead of meeting these expenditures out of the revenue of the country. That is the difference between my hon. friend and myself on this question and I am willing to leave it to the clear judgment of this House as to the better policy to pursue.
My hon. friend spoke at some length upon the dumping clause of our tariff. I could not say from the statement of my hon. friend whether he was in favour of our policy or against it. I gathered that two years ago when my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) made a speech rather against it, my hon. friend was rather in favour of it. But since that time it seems to me that my hon. friend has changed his mind and that he is now rather against it. At all events he did not speak enthusiastically about it. He said that I did not speak enthusiastically about it. My hon. friend spoke of my previous statements about the fast Atlantic service. I well remember that on a certain occasion when I was in Toronto I received a telegram from England. I thought it was settled and I so stated to the people of Toronto but I have learned since that occasion that it is not always best to be too sure. But, we have reason

to hope that this policy will bring about the effect for which it has been designed. My hon. friend did not dare to attack it but he rather suggested that it would not be effective because it might be evaded. What feature of the tariff law is there that is not liable to be evaded ? I am sure there will always be some parties in this country and on the other side of the line also who will endeavour to evade the law and I have no doubt that my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson), within six months, or perhaps within a less time, will have to deal with that question. There are parties who will try to get over this law, to defraud the revenue and to prevent the Canadian people from deriving the benefit from it, but that is no argument against the law. If that were an argument against this law' it would be an argument against the whole tariff. My hon. friend cannot point to a single law of any kind whatever and especially one which put a restriction upon free importation or free act of any kind on the part of the community which will not be subject to being evaded, and certainly when a law of this kind is adopted to put a stop to an illegitimate traffic which has been taking place for many years as it has been for the protection of the Canadian manufacturers in the lines of business in which this traffic has been carried on, I have no doubt that great efforts will be made to get over the law. I have no doubt that many hon. gentlemen opposite who are in favour of it are disposed to damn it with faint praise because it comes from this side of the House. Well, we will have to see how it will work. All the business men the country will concede that not only is this a good measure but that it is a bold course which has been taken by the government and one which shows that this government is alive to the necessities of the trade of this country.
My hon. friend also stated that he did not altogether approve-I do not know that I understood him correctly,-of the commission which we were instituting in order to have an inquiry as to how the tariff has been working and as to how it can be improved. My hon. friend did not altogether, as I understood him, condemn the idea, but he did not commend it either. He stands betwixt and between ; he says neither yes nor no. He said :	If you have an inquiry
in order to deal with the tariff why should you deal with the oil duties ? Again on the oil duties my hon. friend did not say very much. He did not attack us on our policy. In regard to the oil duties we did not have any hesitation or difficulty, in deciding upon the policy which we have adopted and I think that policy can be very well defended in very few words. We found the duty on refined oil when we came into office six cents per gallon. We then reduced it by one cent per gallon and this year we have cut the duty in two. We have
reduced the duty on refined oil to two and a half cents per gallon. We have wiped out altogether the duty on crude oil but we have given a bounty of a cent and a half per gallon to the producers of crude oil. Why did we do that ? The reason is obvious and I hope it will commend itself to my hon. friends opposite. The producers of Canadian oil cannot supply the Canadian market. The production in Canada cannot supply more than one-third of the total consumption of oil in Canada. Two-thirds have to be imported. It is a well known fact that if we had wiped out the duty on crude oil without giving any bounty to the producers we would have closed up every oil well that is producing oil in the province of Ontario. There is no doubt as to that. It is a serious question and it is one in regard to which there can be no dispute. I do not think the oil industry has been a very profitable industry to anybody for many years past but it is a well -known fact that thousands if not millions of dollars of Canadian money have been invested in that industry. It so happens that we cannot compete on equal terms with American oil and if we had not given to the producers in the province of Ontario a bounty of one and a half cents a gallon which enables them to keep their wells open the whole of the plants and the -whole of the money which have been invested would have been wiped out and Canada would have lost probably millions of dollars instead of having a profitable industry going on. Instead of having that condition of things, in order to give the consumer the benefit of cheap oil, we thought we were justified in giving a bounty out of the public treasury which will amount to from $150,000 to $180,000 a year. We rely upon the good sense of the people of Canada that they will agree to give this bounty to their fellow citizens who have invested their money in the oil regions so as to keep their industry in operation. This is the justification for our policy and if we are wrong we invite the criticism of our friends on the other side.
Why does not the right hon. gentleman apply that rule to all other industries ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is what we have been doing.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is what we have been doing as I shall show. My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is too critical ; I will be able to show him that we have done that for every other industry. At all events, if we have not the approbation of his leader, we have his own approbation with regard to this particular item of our policy because my hon. friend has approved of it.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He approved of it, and I understood his leader to say

that he was not sure whether or not our policy would decrease the price of oil. My information at the present moment is, that the day after the Minister of Finance delivered his budget speech the price of oil was reduced two and a half cents a gallon to the consumer, and that is the best justification for the policy we have adopted.
How long will you continue the bounty to the producer ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is no time limit contemplated in the resolutions. The policy of the government is to maintain it, so long as the conditions require that it should be continued.

After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker ; we are now face to face with an amendment moved by the leader of the opposition, no doubt with the full concurrence of his party, by which the people of Canada are invited to abandon the policy under which this country has thrived and prospered this last seven years. It is now seven years since the Minister of Finance introduced the tariff which has since been known, and will long continue to be remembered by grateful generations as the Fielding tariff. When the Minister of Finance concluded his first budget speech in 1897, we on this side of the House believed that he had opened a new page in the fiscal history, nay, in the general history of Canada. Great were our expectations then, but greater still has been the reality. Under the Fielding tariff, Canada has developed as no country has developed during the same period!. Our, languishing industries have been revived ; new industries have sprung into life ; agriculture, long depressed and sore tried has flourished ; trade has more than doubled in volume ; the revenue has become unprecedentedly buoyant; hope, confidence, national pride have risen high in the hearts of Canadians. The name of Canada, up to that moment scarcely known beyond her borders has since become a synonym for national progress, and an object of attention from the whole civilized world. True it is that during those seven years this tariff has been the object of constant carping and cavilling on the part of the opposition-an opposition which styles itself His Majesty's loyal opposition, but which never loses an opportunity to arouse passions and prejudices. It is also true, Sir, that during these seven years, the opposition has been forced to shift its ground more than once. Scarcely had the Minister of Finance uttered the last word of his budget speech in 1897, than the leader of the opposition arose and with tears in his eyes and indignation in his voice, he denounced the tariff which had been introduced as the death knell of the industries of Canada. In

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
.
the face of what followed it was absurd to maintain that line of attack, and as Canada developed and prospered the opposition had to change their batteries and adopt other means of attack. They passed without compunction from one extreme to another ; from the extreme of vilification to what must have been to them the extreme of laudation, for they said that the tariff was simply their own tariff, the old national policy under another name. When the absurdity of this position became manifest, once more they changed their ground, and then stated that if the country had prospered it was not due to the tariff, but was the work of Providence. That has been repeated all through this debate. Well, Sir, I may tell my hon. friends opposite, that no one on this side of the House will take exception to that argument. We recognize that we owe an immense debt (of gratitude to Providence. Providence has blessed us with good crops, good prices, buoyant revenue and increased trade, and I may say without boasting that for these blessings our prayers go forth to Heaven every day. I would like to invite hon. gentlemen opposite to join with us in those prayers, did I not fear that their gratitude would be insincere. In human affairs we know that Providence acts through human agencies and we are inclined to think that these gentlemen opposite cannot forgive Providence, because it suited Providence to choose us poor Grits to be the instruments through which to lavish His bounty upon this fair land of Canada, of which my hon. friends opposite are the fortunate though disgruntled citizens. In the 16th century there lived in France the celebrated surgeon, Ambrose Pare. He was eminent in his profession, and he was as modest as he was eminent. One day he was called to the bedside of am illustrious patient, and he was lucky enough to bring him back to life and health. On being asked how he managed to do it, he simply uttered these words : ' I treated him, God cured him.' My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, who is also a modest man, who adds modesty to all his other good qualities, was called in 1897 to the bedside of a patient endowed with a strong constitution, but whose constitution had been much impaired by empirical treatment ; and in the same way, he may say of this patient,
' I attended him, God cured him.' Mr. Speaker, hon. gentlemen, on the other side of the House tell us, and repeat every day, that if the country is prosperous, it is all the work of Providence ; yet they are not willing to leave that work in the hands of Providence. They think-it is one of their pet notions-that they can perform the work much better than Providence can. This is the object of the amendment which they have placed in your hands ; and they expect that the Canadian people will take the work out of the hands of Providence in which they have placed it, and put it

into theirs. Well, I do not expect that because Providence is with us, the Canadian people will be against us, though that apparently is a reason why the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House should be against us. Sir, when we adopted the tariff which has been in force since 1897, we did not act from any set notions ; we did not pretend to give expression to any fad or any stereotyped theory ; but we thought it was a tariff well suited to the needs of the country. We thought it was the application of practical notions to the requirements of all classes of ' our population. It was a tariff which was devised first of all to promote the revenue, and next, as an incident, to protect Canadian productions against foreign productions. It never entered our minds that this tariff was to be eternal-that it was to, like the laws of the Medes and Persians, be there for ever. .My hon.' friend the Minister of Finance stated on more than one occasion that the tariff should be revised from time to time as necessity required. He has been invited more than once to revise the tariff -invited by friends, invited by foes. Up to this year my hon. friend has resisted all such invitations ; but to-day there are signs of the rising storm-signs of the rising of economic disturbance ; and it would be well to trim our sails and set the ship, so as to have her ready to weather the storm. This is what is done by the changes this year. They are reform, and nothing but reform. My hon. friend the Finance Minister has stated that they do not go as far as he would like ; and he has stated the course he intends to follow with reference to future changes. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition also proposes changes of the tariff, but very different changes. He does not propose to reform ; he proposes to revolutionize. He practically says to the people of Canada, let us undo what we have done in the last seven years ; let us tear out our tariff. Sir, it is always an easy task to destroy. The difficulty is to build up again. What is proposed by my hon. friend 7 He proposes to destroy the tariff, but what will he substitute for it ? My hon. friend wants what he calls adequate protection. But what is adequate protection ? He says it is-no, he declines to tell us. Again, I make a slip : but I am sure I can correct it without a murmur from the other side of the House. He has not declined to tell us what adequate protection means-he has not declined, because he cannot do it. He cannot any more tell us what is adequate protection, and what is not, than he can tell us the difference between tweedledum and tweedledee. The two things are not definable. My hon. friend has chosen to keep us in the dark as to his meaning. But though my hon. friend has not told us what he means by adequate protection, at all events we have it from his own lips, from the lips of some of his fol-152
lowers, and from some of his organs, what is at the bottom of his thought, and what he means by adequate protection. In his own mind it means high protection, the very highest protection, American protection, i I am quite warranted in what I say, that what my hon. friend means by adequate protection if he means anything, is the American standard of protection. I find this in the chief organ of the Conservative party, which is to-day, and has been for some months past, I may say for some years past, the Montreal ' Star.' The chief organ of the Conservative party is no longer the Toronto ' Mail,' the Hamilton ' Spectator '. or the Toronto ' World,' but it is the Montreal ' Star,' which is like the sheep of Jacob-all the other sheep have to pay it obeisance. For more than twelve months the. Montreal ' Star ' has had this placard at the top of its editorial page, though I may say it no longer appears :

To the government of Canada.
Give ]tile manufacturers, workingmen, and farmers of Canada the same kind of tariff as that which has made the United States the home of the most prosperous manufacturers, workingmen and farmers in the world.
To the manufacturers of Canada.
Force the government to give you as good a tariff as that which has made the American manufacturers rich. When you get this tariff, pay your Canadian workmen American wages.
To the workingmen of Canada.
Take a leaf out of the hook of the American workingmen. Help your employers to obtain for themselves and for you a Canada-for-Canadians tariff.
To the farmers of Canada.
Profit by the experience of the American farmers, the wealthiest farmers in the world, who support a high tariff and prosper under it and because of it.
This, then, so far as it can be, is the adequate protection of my bon. friend. Therefore, if I am right in my conclusion, and I think I am, we have to choose between the Canadian tariff and the American tariff. If that be the issue, iSir, we on this side of the House are ready to accept it, and we stand by the Canadian tariff. It so happened that in the year 1896, on this continent there) were two general elections, one in the United States and one in Canada. It so happened that in both countries the party in power was defeated. It so happened that in both countries the [DOT] tariff was revised, but it was revised on very different principles. In the United States the tariff was levelled up ; in Canada the tariff was levelled down. In the United States the McKinley tariff, which had been the highest tariff ever adopted by any na-iton, was found to be inadequate-not high enough. It was supplemented by the Dingley tariff, which was still higher. In Canada the tariff of the day was considerably low-

4T76
ered. What was the result ? You have it in the condition of the two countries and the two peoples at the present time. In Canada you have hope, abundance, contentment ; in the United States you have dejection and almost despair. Who can doubt that ? True it is that immediately after the adoption of the Dingley tariff there was a boom, to use an American expression. Everything was booming. Capital flowed into many industries, because a fictitious atmosphere had been created which tempted adventurous men with money. Many industries were denuded of their legitimate capital in order that it might be put into trusts and combines ; and for a time everything was booming in the United States. That was the time when it was stated that England was invaded by American products. That was the time when the Montreal ' Star ' advised Canadian workmen, manufacturers and farmers to adopt the American tariff. That was the time of combines and trusts. During the few years which followed from 1897 up till last year, no less than fifteen combines and trusts were organized in the United States. There was the coal trust, which as you know caused the largest strike which ever took place in any country, which almost created a revolution in the United States ; the iron and steel trust; trusts on farm implements, on chemicals, on sugar, on tobacco, on paper, on glass, on leather, on rubber goods, on electrical apparatus, on radiators, on elevators, on flour, on clocks, and even on beef for some time. But the time came- and it was not very long-when, to use an American expression, the bottom was knocked out of this tariff, and to-day the United States are in a most deplorable condition. The steel trust, for example, which threatened at one time to capture the whole iron and steel industry of the world, is no longer a dangerous competitor, but is struggling for its own existence and has had to dis charge thousands of its operators. The railways, which at one time had not sufficient rolling stock to carry their traffic, are discharging their operatives by the thousands. Within the last few months the Pennsylvania Railway Company-the largest in the States-has discharged no less than 11,000 of its operators, and the New York ' Herald ' fifteen days ago published a statement, which has not been contradicted, that the total number of men discharged by the railway companies since last April is no less than 75,000. We have escaped all this. Our railways are doing good business and so are our manufacturers. Is this then the moment when we should abandon our tariff and'adopt the American tariff ? Nor is this all. Many a time in this House we have been told of what wonderful things another very highly protected country was accomplishing. I refer to Germany. How inhny times have we not heard from the other side of the prosperous condition of the Ger-Sir WILFRID LA CHIRR.
man people, how their trade was invading the world, how German manufacturers were even crushing the trade of old England ? Sir, while it may have been true for a time that Germany was making headway, what is her condition to-day ? Germany followed the example set by the United States, the same example which hon. gentlemen opposite urge us to imitate. Germany adopted a tariff copied largely from the tariff of the United States. And in Germany, as in the United States, trusts and combines ruled the roost. I have a list here of the German trusts and combines in operation in Germany, taken from the consular reports of Great Britain and Germany. There are combines in coal, iron, steel, sewing machines, farm implements, enamelled ware, chemicals, sugar, flour, twine, cotton and woollen yarn, linen goods, ribobns, lead pencils-nothing too small-wood pulp, cement, glass and rubber goods. Unfortunately, there as elsewhere the day of retribution came, and came also the inevitable crash. And in the year 1900, three years ago. Germany began to suffer the first pangs of depression and hard times. The trusts had absorbed a large portion of the capital of her land banks. The land banks commenced to fail right and left, and it is estimated that $200,000,000 of capital was lost by the failures of these banks. Wholesale dismissals of mechanics took place, and the wages of those who remained were gradually lowered. Strikes among the working classes have become a by-word in Germany to-day, and to add to all this, socialism has become rampant in that Country, and yet this is the tariff you are invited to adopt in this country. I do not think that the Canadian people, in the full enjoyment of the results achieved under our tariff, will make the mistake of abandoning it at a time when the country is so prosperous.
But what are the objections raised against our tariff ? I listened this afternoon to my hon. friend, I have listened to this debate very attentively, and have heard the same song sung by every hon. gentleman opposite. We have been told again and again that our relations with our neighbours are not satisfactory, because the balance of trade against us with the United States is yery large. 1 do not deny it. I wish it were otherwise. But if it is in that condition, it is not our fault but theirs, and they have much more to suffer than we. Trade between nations, to be profitable, must be like trade between individuals ; but unfortunately, while we unwilling to trade with the Americans, they are not willing to trade with us. What is the remedy suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite 7 They say, since the Americans will not buy from us, we should not buy from them. I am ready to adopt that policy to a certain extent; and so far as we can dispense with trading with the United States, I should be prepared to do so. But to tell us simply that the balance of trade is

against us is no argument at all. What we must look at is what is behind the balance of trade. To tell us simply that we have a balance of trade against us is an exploded argument, but I shall discuss it because it has been advanced again. It is such an old fallacy that I would have expected it to be discarded long ago. It is a fallacy so glaring and so manifest that I am almost surprised it should be advanced in a House like this ; but as it is pleaded, let us examine it. Bastien, in one of his books, gives a very striking example of how the balance of trade works. A ship left Havre, in France, in 3840 or thereabouts, loaded for New Orleans with a cargo of articles de Paris, valued at 200,000 francs. She reached New Orleans. The freight on these goods amounted to ten per cent and the customs duty to thirty per cent, and they were'sold at twenty per cent profit. The sale therefore realized 352,000 francs. The money was immediately invested in cotton, and the same ship came back to Havre with a cargo of cotton. The cargo was charged in France with ten per cent freight and sold at twenty per cent profit, realizing 464,000 francs. Therefore the shipper made a double profit. He made a profit on his outward cargo of articles de Paris and also upon his inward cargo of cotton. He made over 100,000 francs altogether, and enriched himself and his country to that extent. Buc how did the entries balance in the customs ? In the customs returns there appeared an export value of 200,000 francs and an entry of imports to the value of 352,000 francs, showing thereby a balance of trade against France of 152,000 francs. Therefore, France, according to the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite, was a loser by the operation. But what followed ? That same gentleman, encouraged by his first experience, thought he would tempt fortune again, and he shipped another cargo of the same goods to New Orleans, valued at 200,000 francs. Then an occurrence happened which would cheer the hearts of my hon. friends on the other side. The entry in the customs returns showed an export of 200,000 francs from France, but the ship was lost at sea, and therefore the balance of trade remained in favour of France to the extent of 200,000 francs. This is an apt illustration of the logic of the hon. gentlemen opposite. Let us, Mr. Speaker, be spared this bugbear of the balance of trade because it is simply a nonsensical bugbear. Let us go beyond the figures and examine the situation.
Last year our imports from the United States all told, including bullion and everything else, amounted to the very large figure of 8137.000,000 and our exports only amounted to $71,000,000, showing a very large discrepancy between the two. These are the figures which startle my hon. friends opposite and lead them to exclaim : How can it be possible that we should trade with such a country ? She sells us $137,000,000 1525
worth and will only buy $71,000,000 worth. Is there not something wrong ? Well, let us examine. First of all, out of this $137,000,000 imports from the United States the goods on the free list amount to no less than $69,000,000.
I ask any hon. gentleman on the other side whether we could dispense with any of these goods ? That is the question. Could we, for instance, provide our own raw cotton ? Can -we provide the coal that is needed for use in Ontario ? Can we produce many other of the articles that are required in connection with our industries ? Sir, this free list has been canvassed and compared with the greatest care possible. It has been made to include only raw material or products which the country cannot manufacture at all or cannot manufacture with success. Therefore, I say we cannot dispense with the goods imported from the United States which are on this free list. I have never heard in this House, outside of one item, any exception taken to this free list. The only objection taken is with reference to the matter of corn. We have been told more than once that corn ought not to be on the free list. I take issue at once with our friends opposite on that point and declare my opinion that when we put corn on the free list we conferred on the farmers of Canada one of the greatest boons we could confer upon them. The result has been an increase of the exportation of our animal products, especially the products of our pork-packing establishments. On the other hand, there are some articles that, we are told should be on the free list that are now dutiable. For instance, it is said that coal should be on the free list. We have not thought it possible to make this .change, though I must say there are many good reasons why it would be advantageous to have coal free. It so happens that on this continent the distribution of coal is peculiar. On both shores, the Atlantic and the Pacific the coal beds are in Canada ; in the centre of the continent the coal beds are in the United States, it woukf seem natural under such circumstances that we should have reciprocity in coal. That policy would be to the advantage of the Americans on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, and to those Canadians who live in the interior. Up to the present time we have thought-and in that I think we are supported by hon. gentlemen opposite-that it would be advantageous to put coal on the free list but that we had better keep the duty on it in order to have if possible, the exchange of that commodity in the near or distant future as the case may be. I have here a list of some of the leading dutiable articles coming from the United States to this country. Let me examine briefly some of the articles in that list. The first is coal oil crude and refined, of which we import $1,414,319. Could we dispense with that ? Everybody would be very glad if the

Canadian oil wells could produce all that we need. But they are insufficient. We have tried it again and again, and all that they can furnish is about one-third of our consumption. Therefore, we must have American oil. Then, there is bituminous coal of which we import about $7,000,000 worth. Can the people of Ontario dispense with the coal of Pennsylvania and Ohio ? Of coal dust we import about $400,000. That also is necessary. Of sugar and molasses we import $352,000 worth. Molasses is on the free list. Of locomotives, we import $1,106,521. We have some plants in Canada for the manufacture of locomotives, but, unfortunately, they are insufficient for the requirements of the Country. We must import American locomotives whether we wish to or not. There is a duty on locomotives which must be paid by the Canadian railways whenever they import the locomotives from the United States. They would prefer to buy locomotives in Canada, but they cannot find them here and they must go to the American market for locomotives. Of fertilizers we import $100,000. We cannot dispense with that. Our importation of rails from the United States amounted to only $S6,000. Our rails came chiefly from Europe. In the case of this article, what can we do more than we have done ? We are all anxious to have rails manufactured in Canada. Last year, we put a duty on rails, to become effective as soon as they are manufactured in this country, and we are still waiting for somebody to undertake this manufacture. Oranges and other tropical fruits-our imports were $600,000. We imported of printing paper $246,000 worth. Who can cavil at that 7 We have a duty on printing paper, but it was reduced some years ago. That reduction was made at the prayer of the press themselves, because there was a combine in Canada who were exacting an undue price from them. In order to relieve them from the influence of this combine we reduced the duty, I believe, to fifteen per cent. Altogether this list covers items of importation under duty amounting to $12,000,000. And I am sure that I am within the mark when I say that we have to import these articles from the United States and could not get them from anywhere else. This list added to the free list of $69,000,000 makes a total importation of these articles free or dutiable of over $80, 000,000 where we benefited by the American trade. Now, let us pass to other articles which we import from the United States on the dutiable list. Somebody will ask me -in fact the question was asked this afternoon-why do not you manufacture these articles in Canada ? Sir, we have a tariff against the United States varying from 25 per cent to 35 per cent, an average of 28 per cent. Under that tariff manufactures ought to thrive. I am told, however, that they do not thrive and that we ought to increase the tariff- For my part, I am al-Sir WILFRID LATJRIER.
ways prepared to consider the case of an industry which, being in existence, finds itself pressed by foreign competition. But, when I am told that we should increase the duty with a vague expectation that, by so doing, we shall found an industry and build it up. I am always more or less sceptical. I am sceptical because of the experience of the Canadian people as I have seen it exemplified in this House. I remember the occasion-I was sitting on the other side of the House ; it wTas in 1885 or 1887-when Sir Charles Tupper then acting as Minister of Finance introduced what was called the iron policy. He more than doubled the duties that had, up to that time, been paid on iron, and he made bold to say that within five years, Canada would produce all the iron needed for our market. Well, nearly twenty years have elapsed since- that time. In the meantime, not satisfied with the duties placed upon iron, the government of that day introduced legislation to give bounties upon the production of iron. And still the industry did not thrive and prosper. Not satisfied with this, the present government increased the bounties given to iron producers. And what is the result ? To-day, the iron industry of Canada is not able to supply the wants of the Canadian people. It has not been a success. And, though the Canadian people have been paying heavy duties and heavy bounties ever since to establish that industry, yet, after more than fifteen years, we have not reached the goal which i hope we shall reach some day or other. But there is one class of goods which come from the United States, which have come in in a manner which we regal'd as undue and to which we want to put a stop. That is the class of goods that have come in by dumping and slaughtering, by making Canada a dumping ground and slaughter market. We have taken means to prevent that if we can.
My hon. friend rather jeered us this afternoon when he spoke of the policy we have introduced upon this subject. He asked how this policy could be conciliated with the old declarations of free trade. Sir, 1 care not for theories, I want to be practical, and tlfis country must be practical above ail things. Well, Sir, let me say this, and I think I am speaking words which will be understood by everybody, the last word on free trade and protection has not yet been spoken. The conditions of manufacturing are changing every day. The shoemaker, the cabinet maker, all the old craftsmen with which we were familiar in our younger days, have disappeared. Formerly, in every village, boots, and shoes and furniture were made by the people of the locality. The shot-maker, the tailor, the cabinet maker were artisans in every locality. They have all disappeared. To-day these things are all made in large brick manufactories, where there is a great aggregation of capital, where there are thousands and

thousands of men congregated, not only men but women and children also. But if it so happens that through new methods which have been adopted in highly protective countries such as the United States and Germany, if it so happens that large combinations engaged in manufacture, after supplying the local market, resort to slaughtering their goods, in this country for example, flooding the market and depriving our' artisans of their work, scattering them, ruining the capital which has been invested in them, I say that under such conditions theory must be abandoned, and it behooves every parliament to try to remedy such a situation. That is the thing we have to do at the present moment.
How will our policy work out, was the question put us this afternoon by my hon. friend. It will work out in this way : As soon as it has been shown to us that an article is being slaughtered in this country, then the Minister of Customs will immediately be able so-to arrange the tariff and so to tax that article as to make the slaughtering of the article impossible of accomplishment. A few months ago I was shown an invoice from Detroit in which an article was set down at a certain price for the American consumer, and at another price, at least 30 per cent below, for the Canadian consumer. This is the regular practice, and I know there are business men in this House who are aware that this is the regular practice, where American shippers, American manufacturers make invoices in which theVe ai'e double prices, a price for the American consumer and a price for the Canadian consumer. I may be told : But is it not to the benefit of the Canadian consumer ? Certainly it is to that extent. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance dealt with that question in his budget speech. It will be to the profit of the individual consumer who may purchase that article at a cheaper price than it can be sold in the United States. But whilst it may be a benefit to the individual Canadian consumer, it is to the detriment of our community as a whole, because it throws a number of our people out of employment, and causqg the destruction of large amounts of capital invested in these industries. At all events, such is the jiolicy we have adopted, and I think it will work well. But I may be told : Why, instead of making a contingent tariff that will go up or down as necessity arises, why not make it absolute so that it will apply under all circumstances ? For this reason, that we do not wish to tax the Canadian people on other industries without any profit to the Canadian consumer ; therefore we have preferred, instead of adopting a regular, absolute, and tyrannical tariff, to adopt a contingent tariff that will go up or go down as the circumstances of the case may require. At all events, this is an ex- . periment. It is not only an experiment, but it is a new device which has been introduced into the world, because I do not think that anything like it has before been tried anywhere. We invite the fair consideration of our friends on the other side of the House to this policy. We have prepared it according to our best judgment, and we think it ought to work satisfactorily, and will destroy an evil which is becoming manifest in modern industrial conditions. We have in ' this country, as in other countries, and indeed in all countries, manufactures carried on under a customs tariff, whereby a fictitious atmosphere is created, artificial conditions, under which manufacturers are carrying on their operations. They have a right to' expect therefore that the condition of things under which they have built up their manufactures shall be maintained. This policy which we have adopted w'e believe will commend itself to the fair 'judgment of the Canadian people the more it is debated and discussed.

not imitate any other nation, we were the originators. Of all the fallacious theories that was ever advanced, perhaps the most fallacious is this balance of trade theory. The Prime Minister referred to it to-night and explained it excellently well. With the example of Great Britaift before their eyes, where the imports have exceeded the exports, by millions, and tens of millions, for the past half century, and where the wealth of the country has at the same time enormously increased, one would think that bon. gentlemen opposite would be less dogmatic in their declarations. Take again, the case of Ireland, where the exports have exceeded the imports not for half a century only but for centuries, where the very life-bloo,d of the nation and people were drawn upon to pay the rents to the absentee landlords, where everything was goint out, and nothing practically coming in, and you have, as you must have, because of this, one of the poorest, if not the poorest nation in Europe. They tell us that the United States' export have for years been greater than their imports, and in consequence of this they have grown wealthy. No, not in consequence of this, but because of the rapid development of their almost illimitable national resources, and because of the enormous inflow of population : with perhaps, some other contributing causes. So long- as their exports exceed their imports, their foreign trade is. not and cannot be in a healthy condition, as I think a few concrete examples will abundantly prove. Suppose I buy a cargo of wheat consisting of say 100,000 bushels for $1 per bushel, which I ship to Liverpool or London and sell at a profit of 50 cents per bushel. I then take my money, $150,000, and invest in merchandise, which I bring to this country. I have certainly made a profitable trade, and what is profitable for me is ijrofitable for my country. But the outward or export entry is 50 per cent less than the inward or import entry : and, of course, the reverse of this would alk>
be true : if I sold at a loss, the export entry Mr. J. j. HUGHES.
would be greater than the import entry, and what would be my loss would also be my country's loss. Now, Sir, it will make no difference if I do not reinvest my money, but bring it back in the form of gold or exchange. Some other man, who' is an importer, by reason of my profitable transaction, would be able to import a larger bill of goods than it would under other circumstances be possible for him to do, because the country would have the gold or exchange to pay for them. All trade is, in its last analysis, barter, and it changes not the essence of the transaction whether money is or is not used to facilitate the trade ; and any nation importing more than it is exporting, and not parting with its gold reserve, must be trading at a profit. All profit in trade is made by taking things from where they are relatively cheap to where they are relatively dear, and all nations of the world could therefore profitably made with one another and the imports of all be greater than the exports of all. Why, even a red Indian who traded furs for blankets, rifles, powder and other things be required, would know that the fewer furs he parted with and the more blankets, rifles, powder, Ac., be received, the richer he would be. In other words, the smaller his exports and the greater bis imports, the better for him ; and what is true of the individual is in all such cases true of the nation. When two nations make war on each other and blockade each others ports, it is not for the purpose of preventing exports but preventing imports. For they well know that they can inflict greater damage upon their enemy by preventing them from bringing things in rather than sending things out. If we fully realized this, if we fully realized what very dependent beings we are, all depending upon one another, and the greater that interdependence the greater our civilization, we would, I think, try to act differently. Only savage tribes and barbarous nations want to or can afford to live by themselves. Why do we dig canals, bridge rivers, construct railways and subsidize steamship lines, if not to trade -with our neighbours and other nations ? Would we go to all this expense and exertion if this trade were not good for us V If other nations will not give us their goods for nothing, and they are not likely to do that, our imports, under ordinary con-*ditions, can never injure our business, because we must make or produce things to give in exchange for the things we receive. But our hon. friends opposite ask us- and they ask, too, in a tone that implies that in their opinion no satisfactory answer can be given-what has the Liberal government done for Canada ? To my hon. friends opposite I would therefore say : If you seek a monument, open your eyes and your ears, and look around you. Be not as those who have eyes and see not, ears and hear not. Open the Trade and Navigation Returns and the Trade and Commerce Returns, and read and understand them. To be more specific, the Liberal government have reduced the taxation by some thirteen per cent, thereby freeing the trade of the country to that extent, and leaving some miilliioDis in the pockets of the taxpayers of the country. They have completed the canal system, giving us fourteen feet of navigation from the head waters of the great lakes to tide water. They have made many valuable and substantial improvements in the harbours and channels of the great lakes themselves as hon. gentlemen opposite well know. They have deepened, lighted and buoyed the St. Lawrence river, the great artery of our commerce from the interior to the ocean. They have built w'harfs and piers and dredged the harbours and rivers of the maritime provinces, thereby enabling us to trade more easily with one another and with the outside world. They have also in many places constructed boat harbours, where the property of that hardy and most deserving class of our population the fishermen, who pursue their arduous calling on the Atlantic coast and in the gulf of St. Lawrence, can be protected from danger, and they are developing our fisheries. They have extended the Intercolonial from Point Levis to Montreal and to points in the maritime provinces, and made it a first-class up-to-date railway, and not the one-horse affair, that it was in the days of the Conservative administration. They have immensely aided and developed the great agricultural interests of the country. They have given us penny postage and a surplus, where formerly we had a deficit of three-quarters of a million dollars. They have given us peace, concord and national amity, or at least tried to do so, where formerly we had discord, strife and national enmity. They have brought about such a condition of things in Canada that the best blood of Europe and America is flocking to our shores; and, perhaps best of all, they have practically stopped the exodus. Our own young men and women are now remaining at home to build up a strong Canadian nationality under the protection of the British flag. Canada is no longer typified by Rachel of old, who wept for her children, and would not be
tinction to-what shall I say ?-to the Conservative government that we had between 1878 and 1896, whose record, beginning with the Pacific scandal, ended with the shocking revelations of 1891 and 1892, and the unseemly and disgraceful scenes of 1895 and 1896, when Canada was pointed to with the finger of scorn by the independent press of the mother country ; when her name became a synonym for dishonesty, malfeasance and corruption in high places ; when Canadians had reason to hang their heads in shame, until finally the junta turned upon and rent each other, calling one another by the most opprobrious epithets the English language could supply. I am sorry my hon. friend Mr. Ross, of Victoria, is not in, because he is a very nice old gentleman, and I would like him to hear what I say. He was very anxious, I am told, to be the candidate again, though a very old man, and he took occasion to write a letter to a newspaper, which I have no doubt the Minister of Finance has seen, in which he pointed out that although his constituency had a population of a little less than 11,000, he had succeeded in getting twenty-eight appropriations for it -for breakwaters, wharfs, refuges for boats, and one thing and another-amounting to
8110,000,	or 810.50 a head for every man, woman and child in it. If that is the way public moneys are frittered away, no wonder we are not reducing the debt very much. It is not very creditable to find that these people have had 8130,000,000 more than the late government were getting, when they said the late government were bleeding the country white, and they have not reduced the public debt more than $1,000,000.
To which of those appropriations does the hon. gentleman object ?
I am not sufficiently familiar with the locality, but I would like to know to which ones the Postmaster General can point as necessary.
We say they are all necessary.
I am afraid the hon. gentleman is speaking without knowledge or is carried away by his party views.
Will the hon. gentleman say that any are unnecessary 7
I think the hon, gentleman could do that himself.

I will indicate the necessary ones and that is the whole list.
*Mr. WiLSON. I recollect that when the Grand Trunk Pacific was being discussed, not one hon. gentleman opposite could tell within ten million dollars what it would cost. They made some statement about its costing only $13,000,000, but that was absurd. I shall take occasion, before the session closes, to call the attention of tne Prime Minister to a rubber combine. There are 74 wholesale rubber jobbers, and there is not one who does not belong to the association. They have the guarantee of the

manufacturers not to sell to any one who Is not a member of the association. If the Minister of Finance is prepared to take the matter up, I will furnish him with the bylaws and report of the last annual meeting and the sheets they give their travellers when they send them on the road. Each one has to make a declaration, and his travellers also, every two or three months- they used to have to make It once a month- that he will stand by the arrangement entered into or forfeit a check for $500, which he has to put up. They have raised their prices anywhere from ten to twenty per cent, and besides that they have lessened the discount from two to seven per cent.

I shall not pursue that any further, but shall take up another matter, and that is the purity of the Liberal party as exhibited in the courts. In my own riding we have had a good many contests, and the Liberal party have never been able to unseat a Conservative member in Lennox since 1882. We have unseated three or four Liberals it not more, but although the Liberal party put in their protests at our last local election, and although our member had only three of a majority, they were finable to unseat him. I have taken up a good deal of the time of the House and have not got through more than one-half what I intended to say, but I am certainly in favour of a change somewhat different from that proposed by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and I think he will find it in the resolution proposed by the leader of the opposition.
